children: By Pritam Biswas

Institutional-investor enthusiasm for data-center stocks waned in the third quarter, with more funds completely exiting positions than opening new ones, while buying of artificial intelligence and semiconductor stocks remained positive but concentrated, regulatory filings showed.

At least 138 funds completely sold their data-center positions during the period, compared with 119 that initiated new positions, according to a Reuters analysis of nearly 6,400 Securities and Exchange Commission 13F filings from pensions, hedge funds, wealth managers and others.

The number of institutional investors that were holders of a group of eight publicly traded companies identified by Reuters as among the largest data-center stocks declined to 3,392 from 3,411 in the previous quarter.
Heavy investment in AI infrastructure and computing capacity led by technology companies ranging from Nvidia
to Microsoft
earlier this year had lifted a slew of stocks related to data centers, including Vertiv Holdings
and Digital Realty Trust

as well as utilities and power stocks that stood to gain from such facilities' surging electricity needs. But growing concerns over an existential threat from AI and a potential slowdown of its development, coupled with macro pressures, dampened enthusiasm for that trade.
The retreat was sharpest in utilities and power stocks, with 212 funds exiting such positions, more than double the 96 that initiated new ones, the filings show.
SEMICONDUCTOR BUYING REMAINS POSITIVE
By contrast, institutional investors remained net buyers of semiconductor and AI stocks, although new positions only slightly outpaced complete exits.

In semiconductors, 2,951 funds, or 51% of those holding the stocks across both quarters, increased their positions, while 2,584, or 44.7%, reduced them. Just 77 funds initiated new positions, against 69 that exited completely. AI stock holdings tracked a very similar pattern, with the total number of institutional holders of such shares rising by just 33.

Shares of AI companies took a hit globally in the third quarter after top industry executives warned of existential risks from the technology, shaking confidence in a sector whose massive infrastructure spending has driven world stock markets to record highs.
THIRD POINT, TIGER GLOBAL SHIFT HOLDINGS
Billionaire investor Daniel Loeb's hedge fund Third Point dissolved its entire stake in Amazon
and semiconductor manufacturing equipment maker ASML, according to a regulatory filing showing what the firm owned on September 30. It also cut its stake in Google parent Alphabet
by 82.9%. However, the fund built stakes in chip designer Nvidia and Microsoft during the third quarter, the filing shows.

In November, as markets were tumbling and investors worried about a possible unraveling of the so-called AI trade, Loeb told his own investors that he had cut risk. Third Point cut its semiconductor- and data-center-adjacent positions, as well as the hyperscalers, according to a letter seen by Reuters. Loeb did not name the positions he cut but said current conditions call for "significantly lower gross and net exposures and a more selective approach."
Tiger Global cut its stake in Applied Materials

, which is a supplier of equipment used in semiconductor manufacturing. The hedge fund also significantly cut its stake in Alphabet, Meta Platforms and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. It also cut a little over 4% of its stake in Amazon. Appaloosa Management built stakes in Applied Materials and software maker Oracle.
Appaloosa increased its stakes in Nvidia, Elon Musk's SpaceX
, semiconductor company Micron Technology
and ASML. It completely sold off its stakes in Advanced Micro Devices
and Broadcom
, whose custom AI chips are used by companies including Meta, Google and OpenAI.
Tiger Global declined to comment. Appaloosa did not immediately respond to a request for comment. All of them filed their quarterly 13Fs on Monday.

Institutional investors are required to disclose their equity holdings in the quarterly 13F filings with the SEC. These offer a snapshot of positions at quarter-end but do not disclose the reasons behind investment decisions.
The third quarter of 2026 ended on September 30, over a month before the Nasdaq selloff after the US midterm elections.
